messages.content: What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?

message.content: The last common ancestor of a lion (Panthera leo) and a zebra (Equus quagga) is the last common ancestor of the super‑order **Laurasiatheria**, which includes both the order Carnivora (lions) and the order Perissodactyla (zebras). This ancestor lived roughly **90–100 million years ago** during the late Cretaceous period, before the diversification of the major mammalian lineages that led to modern placental mammals.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) are both mammals, but they belong to different orders: lions are Carnivora, zebras are Perissodactyla. Their common ancestor would be at the level of the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, or maybe earlier. But we can give a more precise answer: The last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). That ancestor lived around 100 million years ago. So the answer: The last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, which lived about 100 million years ago. Alternatively, we could mention the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both orders, which is the last common ancestor of the superorder Laurasiatheria. Actually, Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria is the common ancestor. That ancestor lived about 90-100 million years ago. So answer accordingly.
